# The whole plan, in one read

**1,146 hours across ten months — 8 August 2026 to 31 May 2027 — to go from "can code" to "gets
software engineering offers".** This page explains the shape of it. Every subject then has its own
page with the same structure, and the day-by-day plan turns all of it into three or four concrete
tasks per day.

---

## Three kinds of resource, everywhere in this guide

| Label | What it is | The mistake it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| **LEARN** | Where knowledge comes from — a book, a course, written notes | — |
| **PRACTICE** | Where you apply it and *something other than you* says whether you were right | Reading about a subject and believing that counts as knowing it |
| **REFERENCE** | Look-up material. Never read front to back | Spending twenty hours reading an encyclopaedia |
| **TEST** | The specific checks that mean a subject is finished | Polishing a subject you enjoy while a harder one goes untouched |

**A subject with no PRACTICE row is a subject you will fail an interview in.** That single rule
shaped every list in this guide.

---

## The problem this plan is built to solve

Most preparation advice is a list of topics. Lists of topics are not the hard part — knowing which
of them matter, in what order, and when to stop, is.

So this plan was not assembled from advice. **240 interview write-ups from students at one
engineering college were read and counted** — what was actually asked, at what stage, by which
companies. Every hour below is allocated against that evidence rather than against a feeling.

Two things that measurement changed:

- **Almost everything gets asked less at the full-time stage than at the internship stage** —
  operating systems, C++, even algorithms. Two subjects do not: **databases** stays flat, and
  **system design** actually rises. That is why databases gets 90 hours and system design gets 46
  even though neither feels as urgent as algorithms.
- **The failure point for most people is not the interview room. It is the online test before it.**
  Being good at algorithms and being able to convert that under a 90-minute clock with no debugger
  are different skills, and only one of them is usually practised.

---

## How the year is shaped

**Everything runs every week.** This is the single most important structural decision here, and it
is deliberately inefficient.

The obvious plan is to study one subject at a time — a month of databases, then a month of operating
systems. It is more efficient and it is wrong, because hiring does not wait for you. Clear an online
test on Monday and the interview is on Thursday, and it will ask about databases, operating systems,
class design and your own projects — whatever month you happen to be in.

So **every subject an interviewer could ask about tomorrow carries a non-zero allocation every single
week**, and depth rotates on top of that permanent baseline. Fourteen to sixteen subjects are live in
any given week.

**What that costs, stated plainly:** keeping a subject warm all year costs roughly 50% more hours
than studying it in one block. Algorithms gives up about 26 hours to fund it. That is the right
trade, because a subject you cannot answer *on the day* is worth zero however many hours were
scheduled for it later.

---

## Where the hours go

| Hours | Subject | Why it gets that much |
|---|---|---|
| **382** | Algorithms & contests | The gate. 95% of internship interviews, 77% of full-time ones. Nothing else is close. |
| **98** | Building a real backend service | One project that makes 20 separate CV claims true at once |
| **93** | Databases & SQL | 55% of interviews and — uniquely — it does not decline at the full-time stage |
| **73** | Designing one class or small system | The thing that ends interviews you were otherwise passing |
| **64** | AI retrieval & evaluation project | The one area of genuine current demand you can enter cheaply |
| **58** | Defending everything on your CV | Every line on it is a question you have agreed to answer |
| **53** | Python & its data libraries | The prerequisite for both projects |
| **51** | C++ and how the machine runs it | Where crashes and silent wrong answers come from |
| **46** | Designing a whole system | The only subject that *rises* from internship to full-time |
| **44** | Systems programming project | Build your own grep, shell, HTTP server |
| **42** | Operating systems & concurrency | Asked constantly; usually answered from memorised definitions |
| **37** | University coursework | Exam-pass level, no further |
| **31** | Debugging under time pressure | The first thing fixed, because it is the thing that fails first |
| **~90** | Everything else | Aptitude, behavioural, tools, networks, AI vocabulary, Java |

---

## The eight phases

| # | Months | Focus | The point of it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aug | **Debugging** | Fix the thing that makes you lose tests you knew how to pass |
| 2 | Sep | **C++ internals** | Understand the crashes rather than fear them |
| 3 | Oct | **Databases + Python** | The highest-value subject, and the language the projects need |
| 4 | Nov | **Databases + start the backend project** | Finish databases properly; the project gains weight |
| 5 | Dec | **Class design + the project** | Start with an LRU cache — the question that ends the most interviews |
| 6 | Jan | **Ship the backend project** | ⭐ Live URL, tests passing. The last high-capacity month |
| 7 | Feb–Mar | **System design + the AI project** | Capacity drops. The subject that rises at the full-time stage |
| 8 | Apr–May | **CV defence + systems project** | Consolidate. Start nothing new |

**The real deadline is 1 February, not May.** Capacity drops from 30 hours a week to 23 after that,
because of coursework load. Phases 1–6 carry most of the plan; phases 7 and 8 are consolidation, not
new ground.

---

## Four rules that run all year

1. **One competitive-programming contest every week, and always solve afterwards the problems you
   could not solve during it.** The contest measures you; the solving-afterwards is where you
   improve. A contest without it counts as half done.
2. **Compile with the safety checks always on.** For C++, that means address and undefined-behaviour
   sanitizers plus the standard library's debug mode. This is a twenty-minute setup that prevents an
   entire category of lost tests.
3. **A weekly baseline is a floor, not a suggestion.** Half an hour a week on class design means one
   problem a fortnight — that is what keeps you able to answer on the day.
4. **Log the hours you actually did, and re-plan against those, not against what you intended.**

---

## If you fall behind — decided now, not later

Nobody hits 30 hours a week every week. The failure mode is not collapse; it is planning at 30,
delivering 22, and letting the shortfall silently eat whatever was scheduled last. So the cut order
is fixed in advance:

**Cut in this order:** problem volume in algorithms → coursework beyond exam-pass → the smaller
subjects (tools, networks, AI vocabulary) → the CMU database course → the scope of the AI project.

**Never cut:** debugging, the weekly contest, class design, the backend project, or CV defence.
Those are the gate, the goal, and the two things that have already cost real offers.

---

## How to actually use this

**Each morning, open the day's tasks.** Three or four items, each with a link, a time, and — the
first time a resource appears — an instruction for how to use it. Do them, tick them.

**Read a subject's page before you start that subject**, not while you are in the middle of it. Each
one tells you what the subject covers, why those topics are the whole subject, which resources to use
in what order, which run alongside each other, and the specific checks that mean you can stop.

**The order within a subject matters more than the total hours.** Almost every subject page has a
"do not start this yet, and here is why" note. Those are the most useful sentences in this guide.

# Debugging & Working Under Time Pressure

**~31 hours, front-loaded into the first two months.** The smallest subject here, and the first one,
because it fixes the thing that fails first.

---

## Why this exists as a subject at all

Most preparation assumes the problem is *not knowing enough*. Often it is not. You can know the
algorithm, write the right approach, and still score zero — because the program crashed on a case you
could not see, or you spent forty of your ninety minutes hunting a bug that a compiler flag would
have pointed at in one second.

This is a real example, and it is why this subject leads the plan: an online test lost to a
segmentation fault and a subtly wrong comparison function, in a problem whose approach was correct.
No amount of extra algorithms study fixes that. **Twenty minutes of setup does.**

Online tests are also where most candidates are eliminated — before any human sees their work. So
the first fix in this plan is not a topic. It is the machinery you sit down with.

---

## What's covered

**Reading failures correctly**
- What each verdict actually means — wrong answer, timeout, crash, memory limit — and the first thing
  to check for each
- Compiler and linker errors: reading them from the top, not the bottom

**Making the computer find your bugs**
- Sanitizers — compiler options that detect out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and undefined
  behaviour at the moment they happen
- Debug modes for the standard library, which catch invalid iterators and inconsistent comparison
  functions
- The silent killers: integer overflow, uninitialised memory, off-by-one at a boundary

**Testing yourself before the judge does**
- A stress-testing harness: a correct-but-slow version, your fast version, a random input generator,
  and a loop that hunts for the smallest input where they disagree

**Working against a clock**
- A template you can type in thirty seconds
- A written log of every mistake you have made, reread before each contest

### Why this is the whole subject

Everything that goes wrong in a timed programming test is one of four things: **you misread the
problem, your approach was wrong, your code was wrong, or you ran out of time.** This subject handles
the last two directly and the fourth indirectly, by removing the time bugs eat.

It is deliberately small and deliberately finite. It is a setup task and a habit, not a field of
study — twenty of these hours are practice, not learning.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | USACO Guide — debugging checklist | **LEARN** | 6 | A fixed procedure for when something breaks |
| 2 | Codeforces guide — sanitizers & debug mode | **LEARN** | 1 | The exact compiler flags, and why |
| 3 | Written debugging notes | **LEARN** | 1 | What each verdict means |
| 4 | Re-solve your own past test papers | **PRACTICE** | 21 | The only honest measure of whether it worked |

---

# The order

## Week 1, day 1: twenty minutes, and do not skip it

Add a compiler alias to your shell that turns on every safety check:

```
alias g++dbg='g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG -Wall -Wextra'
```

Then write a five-line program that reads one element past the end of an array, compile it with that
alias, and watch it tell you exactly which line was wrong.

**That demonstration is the point.** Until you have seen the tool catch a bug you planted, you will
not trust it enough to use it under pressure.

If you do not write C++, the equivalents are `-fsanitize=address,undefined` in C, the race detector
in Go, and running tests under a memory checker in Rust or Java.

## Week 1–2: the four setup tasks, in this order

Each is one sitting, and each depends on the one before it.

1. **The alias, proved to work** (above).
2. **Rebuild your most recent real failure under it.** Take a problem you actually got wrong, make it
   fail again, and watch the sanitizer find it. Write down how long it took. This converts the tool
   from something you were told about into something you have used.
3. **Write the comparison-function rule down.** In C++, a sort comparison must return false when both
   items are equal — using `>=` instead of `>` is silently wrong and crashes deep inside the standard
   library. Break it on purpose, run it with the standard library's debug mode on, and keep the crash
   output.
4. **Build the stress-testing harness.** A slow-but-obviously-correct solution, your fast one, a
   random input generator, and a short script that runs all three until they disagree. Keep it
   somewhere you can paste in thirty seconds.

## Weeks 3 onwards: the practice, which is most of the hours

> **PRACTICE — re-solve your own past test papers** · about 21 of the 31 hours

Set the original time limit. Solve cold, with no notes and nothing open. Then compare against what
you actually submitted at the time.

**The gap between those two is the only honest measure of whether any of this worked.** Not whether
you feel faster — whether the same paper now converts.

## Ongoing, for the rest of the year

- **The safety flags stay on. Always.** They cost a little speed and they save whole tests.
- **The mistake log.** Every time something goes wrong, one line: what happened, what the fix was.
  Read it before every contest. It gets short quickly, which is the point.

---

## What a session looks like

**A setup session (weeks 1–2, 45 minutes):** one item from the four above, finished and working
before you stop. These are not reading sessions — every one of them ends with a program that behaved
the way you predicted.

**A practice session (90 minutes):** one past paper, timed, cold. Then twenty minutes comparing
against your original attempt and writing down what changed.

---

## Honest warnings

**This subject looks trivial and gets skipped.** It is administration, not learning, and there is
nothing satisfying about configuring a compiler. That is precisely why most people do not do it, and
why doing it is worth more than another twenty problems.

**The hours are not the point; the setup is.** If you do the twenty-minute alias task and nothing
else in this subject, you have captured most of the value.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. You can name what each verdict means and what you check first for each, without thinking
2. A deliberately broken program is caught by the right tool, and you know which tool catches what
3. The stress-testing harness exists and you have used it to find a real bug
4. A past paper you previously failed now converts cold, in time, with no crashes
5. The mistake log exists and you actually reread it

# Data Structures & Algorithms

**~244 hours — by far the largest subject here, and the one that decides whether you get to have the
other conversations at all.** Read this together with *Programming Contests*, which is the same
skill measured under a clock.

---

## Why this dominates the plan

Of 240 interview accounts, algorithms appeared in **95% of internship processes and 77% of full-time
ones.** No other subject is within thirty points. It is also the first filter: the online test that
decides whether a human ever reads your CV is almost always an algorithms test.

The uncomfortable implication is that being good at everything else and mediocre here gets you
nothing, while the reverse gets you interviews.

---

## What's covered

**The toolkit**
- Your language's standard containers and what each costs
- Complexity — reading it off code, and estimating whether a solution fits the time limit
- The maths you actually need: modular arithmetic, primes, combinatorics basics

**The core structures**
- Arrays and strings · Hashing · Sorting and the orderings it enables
- Linked lists · Stacks and queues · Heaps (priority queues)
- Trees and binary search trees · Tries
- Graphs — representation, traversal, shortest paths, connectivity

**The core techniques**
- Recursion and backtracking · Binary search, including on the *answer* rather than an array
- Two pointers and sliding windows · Greedy, and how to know when greedy is wrong
- Dynamic programming — the largest single topic in the subject
- Bit manipulation · Range queries (prefix sums, segment trees, disjoint-set union)

**Beyond the standard sheet**
- 0-1 breadth-first search · Offline query processing · XOR tricks on trees and prefixes

**And the part everyone skips**
- Implementing the structures yourself, at least once each

### Why this list is the whole subject, at real depth

The topics above are not a beginner list. The last group — 0-1 BFS, offline queries, XOR on trees —
is what separates someone who solves medium problems from someone who solves hard ones, and it is
exactly the material that standard interview sheets omit.

The test of completeness is simple: take any problem from a real online assessment and it will
decompose into a structure and a technique from these lists. There is no secret extra category. What
varies is *how well hidden* the decomposition is, and that is a matter of practice volume, not of
more topics.

---

## Where you're starting from matters enormously here

This subject is written for someone who is **not a beginner** — roughly 150 problems solved,
comfortable with mediums, has finished most of a standard interview sheet.

If that is you, the diagnosis is almost certainly this: **you have solved a lot of problems with
unlimited time and competed almost never.** The gap is not knowledge, it is conversion under
pressure. The plan below reflects that — it is heavy on volume at a harder difficulty band and heavy
on contests, and light on re-teaching things you know.

**If you are genuinely starting out**, do a standard structured sheet first (Striver's A2Z,
NeetCode 150 — pick one, finish it) and treat this page as what comes after. Everything below assumes
the fundamentals are already there.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Codeforces EDU (ITMO course) | **LEARN** | 32 | Graded lessons on the techniques sheets skip |
| 2 | Competitive Programmer's Handbook | **LEARN** | 30 | One free book covering the whole technique surface |
| 3 | CP-Algorithms | **REFERENCE** | 0 | Encyclopaedia — for looking things up, never reading |
| 4 | Written DSA reference (748 pages) | **REFERENCE** | 0 | Jump to the topic you just got wrong |
| 5 | CSES problem set + a curated sheet | **PRACTICE** | 199 | ~400 problems, harder than you are comfortable with |
| 6 | Weekly rated contests + solving afterwards | **PRACTICE** | 140 | See *Programming Contests* |

Two things to learn from, two things to look things up in, and one enormous pile of practice. **The
199-hour line is the subject.** Everything else exists to make those hours land better.

---

# The order

## Running continuously, from week 1 to the end: problems

> **PRACTICE — CSES problem set and a curated sheet** · ~400 problems · 199 hours

This never stops and never pauses for anything else. Roughly **one hour a day, every day, all year.**

**How to work a problem:** think for a fixed twenty minutes before looking anything up. If you solve
it, still read someone else's solution afterwards — that is where a large share of the learning is.
If you do not solve it in twenty minutes, read the editorial, understand it, close it, and re-implement
from scratch.

**Pick problems above your comfort level.** The single most common way to spend a year on this and
not improve is doing hundreds of problems at a difficulty you already handle. If a problem set feels
smooth, it is not teaching you anything.

## Alongside it, months 1–4: the two learning resources

These two run **in parallel with each other**, not one after the other, because they cover the same
ground from different angles and reinforce each other.

> **LEARN — Codeforces EDU (the ITMO course)** · 32 hours
> Watch a step, then immediately do its exercises. They are automatically graded, so you find out at
> once whether you understood. **Never batch several steps before practising** — that is how you
> convince yourself you learned something you did not.

> **LEARN — Competitive Programmer's Handbook** · 30 hours
> A free book covering the whole technique surface in thirty short chapters. Read a chapter with an
> editor open and **type out its example code yourself.** Reading the code without typing it is the
> standard way to finish this book and gain very little.

**Why both:** the course is graded but narrow; the book is broad but ungraded. Together they cover
the surface *and* check you. Either alone leaves a hole.

## From week 1, forever: contests

> **PRACTICE — one rated contest a week** · see the *Programming Contests* page

This is not a later phase. It starts in week one and runs all fifty-two.

## The two reference resources: never scheduled

> **REFERENCE — CP-Algorithms** and **the written DSA reference**

Neither of these is ever a study session. When a problem needs an algorithm you do not know, you go
to CP-Algorithms for a clean implementation. When you keep getting a topic wrong, you jump to that
section of the written reference. **If you find yourself reading either of them for an hour, you have
mistaken reference material for learning material.**

## Months 5 onwards

Nothing new. The problem volume continues, the contests continue, and the difficulty band rises. The
learning resources are done by roughly month four and are not revisited.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–4 | 6–8 | Codeforces EDU **and** the handbook, in parallel | ~1 problem/day · 1 contest/week |
| 5–8 | 6 | — | Problems at a rising difficulty band · contests |
| 9–10 | 4.6–4.8 | — | Same, plus revisiting anything the checks below fail |

---

## What a session looks like

**A one-hour problem session:** one problem. Twenty minutes of genuine thinking before any help.
Then either solve it and read another solution, or read the editorial, close it, and rewrite from
memory. **One problem properly beats four problems skimmed** — and the second is much more tempting.

**A learning session (months 1–4, 75 minutes):** one Codeforces EDU step plus its graded exercises,
*or* one handbook chapter with every example typed out. Not both, and not either one passively.

---

## Honest warnings

**Volume at the wrong difficulty is the biggest time sink in this whole guide.** Four hundred
comfortable problems will not move you. Aim for a band where roughly one problem in three genuinely
defeats you.

**Reading solutions is not practice, but refusing to read them is worse.** Twenty minutes of real
thought, then read. People lose whole evenings to pride here.

**Do not add more sheets.** The pull to start another curated list when progress feels slow is very
strong, and every additional sheet is more time at a difficulty you have already cleared.

---

## TEST — how to know you're on track

This subject never fully finishes, so these are checkpoints rather than an ending:

1. Every easy and medium problem on real past assessment papers converts **cold, in time, with no
   crashes**
2. 0-1 breadth-first search, offline queries and XOR-on-trees written from scratch with no reference
3. About 400 problems done, with the harder ones genuinely attempted rather than skipped
4. You can look at a problem's constraints and say what complexity is required before thinking about
   the solution

# Programming Contests

**~138 hours — one contest a week, every week, for the whole plan.** This is not a separate subject
from algorithms. It is the same knowledge, measured the way interviews measure it: against a clock,
with no second attempt.

---

## Why this gets its own page

Because it is the part people skip, and skipping it is usually the actual problem.

A typical profile: a hundred and fifty problems solved, and two rated contests all year. That
describes someone who knows a great deal of algorithms and has almost never performed under the
conditions that matter. **The gap is not knowledge. It is conversion.**

An online assessment is a contest. Ninety minutes, three problems, no editorial, no second submission,
and a bug you cannot find is indistinguishable from not knowing the answer. Practising algorithms
without practising that is like preparing for a driving test entirely in a parked car.

---

## What's covered

- Contest format and strategy — reading all problems first, choosing an order, knowing when to abandon one
- Speed: templates, fast input/output, and typing the standard patterns without thinking
- Virtual contests — running a past contest under real conditions when no live one is scheduled
- **Solving afterwards** ("upsolving") — working every problem you failed during the contest
- Rating: what it measures, what it does not, and why it lags real ability by months

### Why this is enough

There is no body of knowledge here. It is a habit with a technique attached. The entire subject is:
compete regularly, do not stop early, and always finish the problems that beat you.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Codeforces rated contests + solving afterwards | **PRACTICE** | 140 | About 40 contests, one a week |

One resource. Nothing else is needed and nothing else substitutes.

---

# The order

## Week 1: register for one, before you feel ready

There is no preparation phase. Pick the next beginner-division contest and enter it. A bad first
contest is data; a delayed first contest is nothing.

## Every week after that: the same two-part routine

**Part one — compete, for the full duration.** Whatever happens. The most valuable habit in this
subject is not leaving early when it is going badly, because that is exactly the skill an assessment
tests.

**Part two — within two days, solve every problem you did not get.** Read the editorial only after
genuinely trying again. Then implement it yourself, from scratch, until it passes.

**Part two is where the improvement comes from.** The contest measures you; solving afterwards is
what changes the measurement. A contest without it counts as half done. If you only have time for
one, do the solving-afterwards.

## When no contest is scheduled

Run a past one as a **virtual contest** — the platform will replay it against the original clock. It
counts.

---

## What a session looks like

**Contest day (2–2.5 hours):** the contest, plus fifteen minutes immediately afterwards writing down
what went wrong — misread the statement, wrong approach, bug you could not find, or simply too slow.
Those four categories are the whole diagnosis.

**Solving-afterwards day (1–1.5 hours):** the problems you missed, one at a time, properly finished.

---

## Honest warnings

**Rating is noisy and lags badly.** Two contests tells you nothing at all. Ten begins to mean
something. Do not read anything into it before then, and do not let a bad run change the plan.

**Chasing a rating number is a worse target than chasing ability.** Deciding to reach a specific
rating pushes you toward contest volume at the expense of technique, and rating is a lagging
indicator anyway. A better target: **every easy and medium problem on a real past paper converts
cold, in time, with no crashes.** Rating then follows on its own.

**The weekly cadence matters more than any individual contest.** Missing one week is fine. Missing
four in a row rebuilds the exact gap this subject exists to close.

---

## TEST — how to know it's working

1. Forty contests entered, and every one of them solved-afterwards to completion
2. You stay for the full duration even when it is going badly
3. Your post-contest notes stop saying "could not find the bug" — that means the debugging subject
   worked
4. Real past assessment papers convert cold and in time

# C++ and How the Machine Runs It

**~51 hours.** Not "learn C++" — you can already write it. This is about the layer underneath: why
programs crash, why they are sometimes silently wrong, and what the compiler actually produces.

---

## Why this is in the plan

Two reasons, and the second is the real one.

**It gets asked.** Roughly half of all interview accounts include language-level questions, and
unusually, that number barely drops at the full-time stage.

**It is where your lost tests come from.** A segmentation fault, an iterator that stops being valid,
a comparison function that is subtly self-contradictory — these do not fail loudly at the line where
you made the mistake. They fail somewhere else, later, and you lose forty minutes. Knowing the
language is not the same as knowing what the machine does with it, and interviews and assessments
both probe the second.

---

## What's covered

**How a program becomes a program**
- Compilation, linking, and what each stage can complain about
- Where things live: stack, heap, static storage, and the cost of each

**Types and memory**
- Expressions, types, and value categories · Pointers and references
- Dynamic memory and ownership · Strings, and why C-style ones behave differently

**Objects**
- Classes and objects · Operator overloading · Inheritance
- Polymorphism, virtual functions, and the table lookup behind them
- Abstract classes and interfaces · `const` correctness

**Modern C++**
- Move semantics — the thing everyone quotes and few can explain
- Casting and exceptions · Templates · The preprocessor and namespaces

**Where the crashes actually come from**
- How the standard containers are built and what each operation costs
- **Comparison functions and strict weak ordering** — the rule whose violation crashes deep inside
  the library
- **Iterator invalidation** — which operations on which container break which references
- A catalogue of undefined behaviour, and what each one looks like when it goes wrong

### Why this is the whole subject, at interview depth

An interviewer probing language depth asks one of three things: *what does this code print*, *why is
this slow or wrong*, or *what happens in memory when this runs*. Those map exactly onto the sections
above.

The last group is where the depth is. Anyone can define polymorphism; being able to say what the
virtual table looks like, which container operations invalidate which iterators, and why `>=` in a
sort comparison crashes, is what separates a strong answer from a memorised one.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Written C++ reference (57 sections) | **LEARN** | 10 | The spine — targeted, never front-to-back |
| 2 | learncpp.com | **LEARN** | 10 | Gap-fill, and its chapter quizzes are the test bank |
| 3 | Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) | **PRACTICE** | 15 | Predict what the compiler emits, then look |
| 4 | Undefined-behaviour drills | **PRACTICE** | 15 | Break the language on purpose, watch the tools catch it |

**Half the hours are practice, and neither practice resource is a problem set.** That is unusual and
deliberate — see below.

---

## The problem this subject has, and how it is solved

**There is no judge for C++ internals.** Nothing tells you your mental model of a virtual table is
wrong. The code compiles and runs either way, and you find out in an assessment.

So the practice here is built to *manufacture* a judge:

- **Compiler Explorer** is a website that shows the assembly your code compiles to, instantly. Write
  a snippet, **say out loud what you think it will produce, then look.** The gap between prediction
  and reality is the lesson. Reading the output without predicting first teaches almost nothing.
- **Sanitizers** (from the debugging subject) are the judge for undefined behaviour. Write code that
  is wrong in a specific way and confirm the right tool catches it.

**Predict, then verify.** That is the entire method for this subject, and it is why 30 of the 51
hours are practice.

---

# The order

## Month 1–2: the two learning resources, interleaved with the first practice

> **LEARN — the written reference** and **learncpp.com**, used together

Do not read either cover to cover. Work through the topic list above, and for each topic use
whichever of the two is stronger on it. Then — this is the important part — **do every learncpp
chapter quiz for the topics you touch.** The quizzes are why that resource is on the list.

> **PRACTICE — Compiler Explorer**, starting in week one alongside the reading

After each topic, write a five-to-ten-line snippet using it, predict the assembly, then check. Start
with something small: what does a range-based loop over a vector become? Roughly 48 of these
predictions over the subject.

## Month 2 onwards: the breakage drills

> **PRACTICE — undefined-behaviour drills**

Once the safety flags from the debugging subject are set up, deliberately write eight kinds of broken
program — read past the end of an array, use a pointer after freeing it, overflow a signed integer,
write a self-contradictory comparison function, invalidate an iterator and then use it — and confirm
which tool catches which.

**Do the comparison-function one first.** It is the single most common silent failure in timed
assessments.

## Months 3 onwards

Maintenance only: about half an hour a week, which in practice means one prediction drill or one
broken program a fortnight. Enough that the reflexes stay.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~2.7 | Written reference + learncpp on weak topics | Compiler Explorer predictions |
| **2** | **~5.7** | **Finish both** | Predictions + all eight breakage drills |
| 3–10 | 0.3–1 | — | One drill a fortnight |

---

## What a session looks like

**A 90-minute session in month 2:** read one topic from your reference and take the matching
learncpp quiz. Then write a snippet using that topic, predict what the compiler will produce, and
check on Compiler Explorer. Ends with you having been right or wrong about something specific.

---

## Honest warnings

**Do not read a big C++ book.** *Effective Modern C++* is genuinely the best book on move semantics
and is 20–30 hours — over half this subject's budget, for a subject where you already have a written
reference. Only escalate there if the checks below fail.

**Watching C++ videos is the lowest-value activity available here.** They re-explain what you can
already read, with no way to find out whether you understood.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. Predict the size of five class layouts you have not seen, correctly
2. Write a comparison function cold, first try, with no compiler errors and no ordering bug
3. Produce all eight kinds of undefined behaviour and have the right tool catch each one
4. Predict iterator invalidation correctly for eight container-and-operation pairs
5. Pass every learncpp chapter quiz for your weak chapters

# Operating Systems & Concurrency

**~42 hours.** Asked in roughly a third to a half of interviews, and almost always answered from
memorised definitions. That is the gap this closes.

---

## Why this is in the plan

Operating systems is the subject people most often "know" without being able to use. Everyone can
define a deadlock. Far fewer can cause one on purpose, look at what the system reports, and say which
of the four conditions they removed to fix it.

Interviewers know this, so the good questions are practical: *what happens when you run this
command*, *why is this process still there after it exited*, *these two threads produce the wrong
answer sometimes — why*.

---

## What's covered

**Fundamentals**
- What an operating system does · User mode versus kernel mode · System calls
- Interrupts, traps and faults

**Processes**
- Process states and the process table · Creating processes, and what a child inherits
- Communication between processes: pipes, shared memory, signals
- Zombie and orphan processes — what they are and how they arise

**Threads and scheduling**
- Threads versus processes · Context switching and what it costs
- Scheduling algorithms and the trade-off each makes

**Getting concurrency right**
- Race conditions · Mutexes, semaphores, condition variables
- The classic problems: producer–consumer, readers–writers, dining philosophers
- Deadlock: the four conditions, and prevention, avoidance, detection
- Tools that find races for you

**Memory**
- Allocation and fragmentation · Virtual memory, paging, page faults
- The translation lookaside buffer, and why locality matters

**Storage and the rest**
- File systems, inodes, directories · Input/output and disk scheduling · Protection and permissions
- Containers as an operating-system feature — namespaces and control groups

**Diagnosing a live system**
- Reading process, memory and file-descriptor state on a running machine

### Why this list is enough

Operating-system interview questions are almost always one of: *what happens when...*, *why is this
slow*, *why is this sometimes wrong*, or *what is this command telling me*. The four practical groups
above — processes, concurrency, memory, live diagnosis — cover all four, and the depth markers are
the last item in each group: zombies, deadlock detection, page-fault behaviour, and reading a live
system.

Deliberately excluded: writing an operating system, kernel internals, and driver development. Those
are a different career, not a different interview.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | OSTEP (free textbook) | **LEARN** | 14 | The best free operating-systems book, with runnable homework |
| 2 | Written OS reference (18 sections) | **LEARN** | 6 | Fast revision before practising |
| 3 | LeetCode concurrency problems | **PRACTICE** | 8 | Six problems where a judge actually runs your threads |
| 4 | Process and thread drills | **PRACTICE** | 12 | Write the small programs yourself |

---

# The order

## Start with the book, but only the useful half of it

> **LEARN — OSTEP**, *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces*

Free online, and unusually readable. Take the chapters on processes, scheduling, memory and virtual
memory, concurrency, and file systems — roughly 29 of them. **Do the homework simulations.** They are
small programs that let you watch scheduling and paging behave, and they are the reason this book
beats every video course on the subject.

> **LEARN — the written reference** runs alongside it, as fast revision before each practice block.

## Then, and this is the part that matters: make it happen on your own machine

> **PRACTICE — process and thread drills** (12 hours)

Write these yourself, in this order — each needs the one before:

1. **Create a child process and wait for it.** Then deliberately *fail* to wait for it, and find the
   zombie in the process list. You have now seen the thing everyone defines.
2. **Pipe data between two processes.** Then replace one of them with a real command.
3. **Write a program with a genuine data race** — two threads incrementing the same counter — and
   confirm it produces wrong answers sometimes. Then run it under a thread sanitizer and watch the
   tool point at the exact line.
4. **Cause a deadlock deliberately**, with two locks taken in opposite orders. Then fix it by
   removing one of the four conditions, and be able to say which one.

> **PRACTICE — LeetCode's concurrency problems** (8 hours, six problems)

The only place in this subject where something else grades your threading. Do them after the drills,
not before.

## Ongoing

About an hour a week. One drill, or re-reading one OSTEP chapter and re-running its homework.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | ~1 | OSTEP chapters + written reference | First process drills |
| **5–6** | **~2.3–2.8** | Remaining OSTEP | Race and deadlock drills · graded concurrency problems |
| 7–10 | ~0.2 | — | Occasional refresh |

---

## What a session looks like

**A 70-minute session:** one OSTEP chapter and its homework simulation, then the matching drill on
your own machine. Ends with a program you wrote doing something you predicted — a zombie appearing, a
race detector firing, a deadlock hanging.

---

## Honest warnings

**This is the subject most often prepared entirely from memorised definitions**, because that works
for university exams. It does not survive one follow-up question in an interview.

**Do not read all of OSTEP.** It is a full course. The chapters listed are the interview-relevant
ones; the rest is excellent and not on the critical path.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. Create a zombie process, find it, and explain exactly why it exists
2. Write a racy program, prove it is wrong, and have a race detector locate it
3. Cause a deadlock and fix it by naming which of the four conditions you removed
4. All six graded concurrency problems passing
5. Explain what happens on a page fault, end to end, without notes

# Databases & SQL

**~90 hours across ten months.** The safest investment in this guide. Almost every software
interview asks about databases, and unlike most subjects, the questions do not become rarer as you
move from internship interviews to full-time ones. They stay exactly as common.

---

## Three kinds of resource, and what the labels mean

Every resource below is labelled. The labels are the most important thing on the page.

| Label | What it is | The mistake it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| **LEARN** | Where the knowledge comes from — a book, a course, notes | — |
| **PRACTICE** | Where you apply it and *something other than you* says whether you were right | Reading about a subject and believing that counts as knowing it |
| **REFERENCE** | Look-up material. Never read front to back | Spending twenty hours reading an encyclopaedia |
| **TEST** | The specific checks that say you are finished and can stop | Polishing a subject you enjoy while a harder one goes untouched |

A subject with no **PRACTICE** row is a subject you will fail an interview in. This one has three.

---

## What's covered

**Foundations — how data is organised**
- Tables, rows, primary keys and foreign keys
- Designing a database from a written description (entity-relationship modelling)
- Creating tables and setting rules about what may go in them (DDL and constraints)

**Querying — getting data out**
- Selecting and filtering rows
- Joins — combining two or more tables
- Aggregation — counting, summing, grouping
- Subqueries and CTEs — queries nested inside queries
- Window functions — calculations across a set of rows without collapsing them

**Design theory — organising tables well**
- Normalisation — splitting tables so each fact is stored exactly once
- Relational algebra — the formal operations SQL is built on

**Performance — why a query is slow**
- Indexing — the structure that makes lookups fast, and what it costs on every write
- Query optimisation and execution plans — what the database decides to do, and how to see it

**Concurrency — what breaks when many people use it at once**
- Transactions and ACID
- Isolation levels and anomalies — the exact ways concurrent users corrupt each other's view
- Locking and deadlock

**Breadth**
- Other architectures, NoSQL, and when a relational database is the wrong choice
- The standard set of questions interviewers actually ask

### Why seventeen topics is the whole subject

Every database interview question is one of five kinds:

1. **"Write this query"** → querying
2. **"Design a schema for this"** → foundations + design theory
3. **"Why is this slow?"** → performance
4. **"What happens if two people do this at the same time?"** → concurrency
5. **"Would you use SQL here at all?"** → breadth

**There is no sixth kind.** The list above covers all five, and it goes to interview-advanced depth,
not introductory depth — window functions, execution plans, multi-version concurrency control and
crash recovery are all in there. Those are the topics that separate a strong candidate from an
adequate one, and they are the last four items rather than optional extras.

What is deliberately *not* here: distributed databases, sharding, and replication. Those are
system-design interview material, not database interview material, and they belong in a different
subject.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A thorough written reference | **LEARN** | 12 | The spine — every topic, once, properly |
| 2 | pgexercises | **PRACTICE** | 8 | Graded SQL, grouped by technique |
| 3 | LeetCode SQL 50 | **PRACTICE** | 6 | Graded SQL in interview shapes |
| 4 | Use The Index, Luke | **LEARN** | 8 | How indexes work and where they stop working |
| 5 | CMU 15-445 lectures | **LEARN** | 20 | How a database is built underneath |
| 6 | Breaking a live database | **PRACTICE** | 24 | Indexes and concurrency, proven by experiment |
| — | The six checks at the end | **TEST** | — | Whether you are done |

Six resources. Adding more is the most common way to spend a year and learn less.

---

# The order — read this part twice

This is the section the rest of the page exists to support.

## Day 1, before you read anything: install a database

```
docker run --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:16
```

That is PostgreSQL — free, open-source, widely used, and unusually good at showing you what it is
doing internally. Everything after today runs against it.

**Why first:** databases are one of very few interview subjects where something outside your own head
can tell you whether you are right. You write a query, it answers. You claim an index will help, you
measure it. Almost every other subject makes you grade your own homework. Do not give up that
advantage by reading for two weeks before installing anything.

No Docker? Install PostgreSQL directly, or use any free hosted Postgres. It only has to be real and
breakable.

---

## Phase 1 · Months 1–2 · about 20 hours · **"Write SQL without looking things up"**

**Two resources, run together, tightly interleaved:**

> **LEARN — the written reference** (the querying half: tables and keys, DDL, SELECT, joins,
> aggregation, subqueries, window functions)
>
> **PRACTICE — pgexercises** (the matching section, immediately after)

**How to interleave them, precisely:** read one topic from the reference — say, joins. Close it. Go
to pgexercises and do that topic's problems until you stop needing to look back. *Then* read the next
topic. Never read two topics in a row without practising the first.

**Also running, in the background, from now until the end:** **PRACTICE — LeetCode SQL 50**, two or
three problems a week. Not a phase. A habit that runs the whole ten months, so your query-writing
stays sharp while you are deep in other things.

**Do NOT start yet:** *Use The Index, Luke*, the CMU lectures, or anything about indexes and
concurrency.

**Why not:** indexes make queries faster. If you cannot yet write the query confidently, "faster" has
nothing to attach to. Concurrency is about two transactions colliding — that means nothing before
transactions are ordinary to you. Starting these early feels productive and teaches almost nothing.

**You are done with Phase 1 when:** you can write a three-table join with grouping, from a schema you
have not seen, without a reference.

---

## Phase 2 · Months 3–4 · about 50 hours · **"Understand what is underneath"**

This is where two thirds of the total time goes, and it has **two tracks that run in a strict inner
order but overlap each other.**

### Track A — Performance · start here

> **LEARN — Use The Index, Luke** (~8 h)
> **PRACTICE — index experiments on your own database** (part of the 24 h)

**Run these together, chapter by chapter.** Every chapter of Luke has a query in it. Run that query
yourself, put `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in front of it, and compare what the book predicted with what your
database reported. Reading Luke without doing this is roughly half as useful.

Then, once, on your own: **find a query where adding an index made things slower**, and work out why.
That single exercise puts you ahead of most candidates.

### Track B — Internals and concurrency · start after Luke, not before

> **LEARN — CMU 15-445 lectures** (~20 h)
> **PRACTICE — deliberately breaking a live database** (the rest of the 24 h)
> **Open alongside: PostgreSQL's isolation documentation** — a lookup, not a reading

**Why Luke before CMU:** Luke explains indexes *practically* — what they do for you and when they
fail. CMU explains them *structurally* — the actual B+tree, the page layout, the algorithms. Coming
to the structure after the practical picture is much easier than the reverse. Doing CMU first is
harder for no gain.

**How to interleave CMU with the breaking:** watch one lecture, then immediately go to the database
and reproduce what it described. After the join-algorithms lecture, write a join and look at which
algorithm your database actually chose. **You never finish a session on the video. You finish on the
database.**

When CMU reaches concurrency control, switch the practice to breakage: open two terminals into the
same database and cause each anomaly on purpose, then set the isolation level that prevents it and
confirm it does. **This** is when the PostgreSQL isolation page becomes useful — you read the
specification for the thing you just caused, not before.

**You are done with Phase 2 when:** the six checks at the bottom of this page pass.

---

## Phase 3 · Months 5–10 · about 20 hours · **"Do not lose it"**

Nothing new. One SQL problem a week, and re-run the six checks once every couple of months. This
subject decays slowly, so the maintenance cost is genuinely small — but it is not zero, and skipping
it entirely means re-learning execution plans in April.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | ~2.3 | Written reference (querying half) | pgexercises · **LeetCode SQL 50 starts and never stops** |
| 3–4 | **~6** | Luke → then CMU lectures | Index experiments → then concurrency breakage |
| 5–6 | ~1.2 | — | One problem a week |
| 7–10 | ~0.5 | — | One problem a fortnight · re-run the checks |

**Two months carry two thirds of the hours.** That is deliberate. Spreading 90 hours evenly across
ten months means never building momentum in any of them.

---

# The resources in detail

### 1. A thorough written reference · **LEARN** · ~12 hours

**What it is:** one complete written source covering all seventeen topics. In my case, my own notes —
182,000 words, and unusually for study notes, about one exercise every 2,300 words. If you do not
have your own, the closest free equivalent is **Stanford's "Databases" course by Jennifer Widom**,
free to audit on edX: five short self-paced courses with quizzes and auto-checked exercises, covering
the relational model, SQL, design theory and constraints.

**How to use it:** topic by topic, in the order listed above, never two topics in a row without
practising the first.

**How much:** all of it, skimming what you already know. Twelve hours assumes you have written SQL
before. From a genuine standing start, budget 25–35.

**A mistake I made, worth naming.** I used a popular exam-revision YouTube playlist and counted it as
"learning done" because I had finished a chunk of it. **Finishing a shallow resource does not mean
you have learned the subject.** Exam-revision videos are built for multiple-choice questions — fast,
surface-level, and they leave you able to *recognise* terms rather than *use* them. Keep them for the
week before a university exam. Do not build on them.

### 2. pgexercises · **PRACTICE** · free · ~8 hours

**What it is:** a free site built around one realistic dataset — a sports club's members, facilities
and bookings — with problems grouped by technique: basics, joins, aggregation, recursive queries. It
checks your answer against the real result.

**How to use it:** immediately after the matching topic in your reference. Write the query before
looking at the hint, every time. When you are wrong, work out why *before* reading the answer.

**How much:** the joins/subqueries, aggregates and recursive sections in full. The basics section can
go fast.

### 3. LeetCode SQL 50 · **PRACTICE** · free · ~6 hours

**What it is:** a curated set of fifty SQL problems in the shapes interviews actually use — much
closer to "here is a schema, answer this business question" than to textbook exercises.

**How to use it:** as a steady background habit, two or three a week from month 1 to month 10. Not as
a block.

**How much:** all fifty, eventually. There is no rush on any individual one.

### 4. Use The Index, Luke · **LEARN** · free online · ~8 hours

**What it is:** a free web book by Markus Winand, entirely about indexing and query performance. It
covers what a B-tree index physically looks like, why one query can use an index and a nearly
identical one cannot, and how to read an execution plan.

**How to use it:** with your database open, running every query it shows.

**How much:** the first half is the essential part — index structure and where indexes stop working.
The later vendor-specific chapters can be skimmed.

### 5. CMU 15-445, Database Systems · **LEARN** · free · ~20 hours

**What it is:** Carnegie Mellon's undergraduate database course by Andy Pavlo, all lectures free on
YouTube. It is about how a database is *built*: how pages are stored, how B+tree and hash indexes are
implemented, how joins are executed, how the planner chooses, how concurrency control and crash
recovery work.

**How to use it:** lectures only, one at a time, each followed immediately by observing that thing in
your own database.

**How much:** about 20 of the 26. Take storage and page layout, buffer pools, B+tree indexes, hash
indexes, sorting and aggregation, join algorithms, query planning and optimisation, concurrency
control, and logging and recovery. Skip the distributed and guest lectures.

**Skip the course projects.** Building a buffer pool, a B+tree and a query executor is excellent and
is roughly 100 hours of C++. That is a serious side project, not part of preparing for interviews.

**This is the most optional part of the subject.** It is what makes you genuinely good at databases
rather than merely ready to be interviewed. If your time gets squeezed, cut this first.

### 6. Breaking a live database · **PRACTICE** · ~24 hours

**What it is:** not something anyone else made. The largest single block of time here, and the part
that actually changes what you can do.

**Three exercises, repeated on different data:**

- **Make a query slow, then fast, and know why.** Load enough rows that timing means something. Run
  a query, time it, add an index, time it again. Then find the case where the index made things
  *worse*.
- **Cause every concurrency anomaly on purpose.** Two terminals, one database. Make one read data the
  other has changed but not committed. That is a dirty read, and you have now seen it rather than
  memorised it. Do the same for the others, then prevent each with the right isolation level.
- **Cause a deadlock and read the report.** Two transactions each waiting on what the other holds.
  The database detects it, kills one, and prints an explanation. Read that explanation properly — it
  is exactly what you would be looking at in a real job.

**How much:** until each one is boring. That is the finish line.

---

## What a session actually looks like

**Phase 1, 45 minutes:** one topic from the reference, then three pgexercises problems using it. Ends
with you typing SQL.

**Phase 2, 90 minutes:** one CMU lecture (~50 min), then straight to the database to reproduce it —
build the index, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before and after, write the numbers down. Ends with you typing
SQL.

**Every session ends in the database.** If a session ended in a video or a book, it was half a
session.

---

## Honest warnings

**Cut CMU first.** If you reach two thirds of your intended hours, drop it before anything else here.
It makes you good; the rest makes you ready, and ready comes first.

**This is the most tempting subject to read your way through** — the material is genuinely
interesting and unusually well written. But interviews ask you to write a query and explain a plan,
and neither improves from reading.

**One realistic dataset beats five toy ones.** Pick one schema and stay with it long enough to know
it by heart. Learning a new toy schema every week is time spent learning schemas.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

Not "have I finished the material". Can you do these six:

1. Write a three-table join with grouping **and** a window function, no reference, in ten minutes
2. Name a query an index made **slower**, and explain why to a non-technical person
3. Reproduce all three concurrency anomalies, then prevent each, naming the isolation level
4. Cause a deadlock deliberately and read its report
5. Clear pgexercises' joins/subqueries, aggregates and recursive sections
6. Re-solve, cold, the database questions you were asked in a past interview

**Six of six means stop.** That is a real instruction. The pull to keep polishing a subject you enjoy
is exactly how the subjects you dislike go untouched.

# Designing One Class or Small System

**~73 hours.** Given a description in English — a parking lot, a lift, a cache, a bill-splitting app —
produce the classes, their responsibilities, and working code, in forty-five minutes.

---

## Why this is in the plan

This is the subject that ends interviews you were otherwise passing.

The pattern is consistent: the algorithms round goes well, the conversation goes well, and then
someone says "design an LRU cache" or "model a parking lot", and the answer is a heap of methods with
no structure. It is not a knowledge failure — most people know what a hash map and a linked list are.
It is that designing and coding under a clock is a separate skill that is almost never practised.

**It is also the most under-practised subject relative to how often it appears.** Reading about design
patterns feels like progress and produces almost none.

---

## What's covered

**Getting the problem right**
- Asking clarifying questions before designing anything — the part that is actually being assessed
- Turning an English description into entities, and entities into responsibilities
- Relationships between objects: has-a, is-a, and when neither is right

**The principles**
- The five SOLID principles, and what violating each one actually looks like in code
- Composition over inheritance, and why the default answer is composition

**The patterns worth knowing**
- Creational: factory, builder, singleton (and why singleton is usually a mistake)
- Structural: adapter, decorator, facade, proxy
- Behavioural: strategy, observer, state, command

**The standard problems**
- LRU cache · Parking lot · Lift system · Vending machine · Chess or tic-tac-toe · Bill splitting ·
  Rate limiter · Logging framework · Notification system · Booking system

**The parts that separate a good answer**
- Extending the design when a new requirement arrives mid-interview
- Making a design thread-safe, and knowing where the contention is
- How you would test the thing you just designed

### Why this list is enough

Every low-level design question is: **take this description, produce classes, defend the boundaries.**
The ten standard problems above cover the shapes — a cache, a state machine, a resource allocator, a
rules engine, an event system. A new problem is always a variation on one of them.

The depth is in the last group. Producing a reasonable class diagram is table stakes. Handling "now
make it work for multiple floors / multiple currencies / concurrent users" is what the interview is
actually testing, because it reveals whether the boundaries were real.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Refactoring.Guru | **LEARN** | 10 | Design patterns, clearly explained, with code |
| 2 | SOLID principles (from the C++ reference) | **LEARN** | 2 | Five principles, once |
| 3 | awesome-low-level-design | **PRACTICE** | 14 | 30 worked problems — attempt first, read after |
| 4 | Timed 45-minute design problems | **PRACTICE** | 20 | The actual skill, under the actual conditions |

---

## The honest problem with this subject

**There is no judge.** No website marks your parking-lot design. That makes it easy to read about
design forever and never find out whether you can do it.

The substitute is **extension**: a design is good if a new requirement can be added without rewriting.
So the practice is built around it — design something, then add a requirement you did not plan for,
and see what breaks. That test you *can* administer yourself, honestly.

---

# The order

## First, before any patterns: one timed problem, cold

> **PRACTICE — build an LRU cache. Forty-five minutes, clock running, nothing open.**

Do this in week one, before reading anything. It will probably go badly. That is the point — it
calibrates everything after it, and it is the single most commonly asked problem in this subject.

## Months 1–4: learn the vocabulary, slowly, alongside practice

> **LEARN — Refactoring.Guru** (10 hours across four months, not a block)

Read one pattern, then **write it out from scratch without looking.** If you cannot, you have read it
rather than learned it. One pattern per session, roughly one session a week.

> **LEARN — SOLID** (2 hours, once)

Read the five principles once. Then find a real violation in your own code and fix it. That is worth
more than any number of examples.

**Do not read all 22 patterns before you start designing.** Patterns are a vocabulary for describing
designs you have already attempted; learned first, they become a hammer looking for nails, and
interviewers can tell.

## Months 2–6: worked problems — attempt, then compare

> **PRACTICE — awesome-low-level-design** (14 hours, 30 problems)

For each: spend twenty minutes producing your own classes and responsibilities **before** opening the
solution. Then read theirs and note specifically what they modelled that you did not.

Reading first teaches you to *recognise* designs. Attempting first teaches you to *produce* them, and
only the second is what the interview asks for.

## Month 5 onwards: the timed canon — the largest and most important block

> **PRACTICE — ten problems, 45 minutes each, then extended** (20 hours)

The order matters, easiest first: **LRU cache → parking lot → vending machine → lift system →
tic-tac-toe → rate limiter → logging framework → notification system → booking system → bill
splitting.**

For each one: 45 minutes on the clock, nothing open, ending with code that runs. Then — and this is
the half people skip — **add one requirement you did not plan for.** Multiple floors. Multiple
currencies. Concurrent users. Whatever breaks is where your design was decorative.

## Ongoing, all year

At least one design problem a fortnight, forever, including in the months where the weekly allocation
looks tiny. **Half an hour a week means one problem a fortnight, and that is exactly what keeps you
able to answer on the day.**

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | ~2 | Refactoring.Guru, one pattern a week · SOLID once | The cold LRU attempt · first worked problems |
| 3–4 | ~1 | Remaining patterns | Worked problems continue |
| **5–6** | **~4–6** | — | **The timed canon: ten problems, each extended** |
| 7–10 | ~0.4 | — | One problem a fortnight, forever |

---

## What a session looks like

**A learning session (45 minutes):** one pattern read, then written from memory. If the from-memory
version does not compile, read it again.

**A timed session (90 minutes):** 45 minutes designing and coding cold, then 20 minutes adding an
unplanned requirement, then 15 minutes writing down what you would do differently. **The last 35
minutes are worth more than the first 45.**

---

## Honest warnings

**Reading design patterns is the most comfortable non-progress available in this whole guide.** The
material is well written and satisfying, and it converts to nothing unless you design something
immediately afterwards.

**Do not memorise the standard problems.** Interviewers vary them deliberately. What transfers is the
habit of clarifying first, naming responsibilities, and defending boundaries — not a remembered class
diagram for a parking lot.

**Forty-five minutes is not a suggestion.** Designing without a clock is a different, much easier
activity, and it is not the one being tested.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. LRU cache written cold, in 20 minutes, working, with the eviction policy correct
2. Any of the ten canonical problems designed and coded in 45 minutes
3. An unplanned requirement added to one of your designs **without rewriting it**
4. The five SOLID principles named, with a real violation you found and fixed for each
5. You ask clarifying questions before designing — automatically, without being prompted

# Designing a Whole System

**~46 hours.** Not one class — an entire product. "Design Twitter." "Design a URL shortener that
handles a billion redirects a day."

---

## Why this is in the plan, despite feeling premature

**It is the only subject that gets asked *more* at the full-time stage than the internship stage** —
roughly 26% of internship processes and 32% of full-time ones. Everything else declines.

That single fact is why it earns 46 hours from someone who is not yet a senior engineer. It is also
the subject where candidates most often have nothing at all to say, which makes the marginal value of
being merely competent unusually high.

---

## What's covered

**The reasoning**
- Estimation: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth — arriving at numbers out loud
- Where to put things: load balancers, content delivery networks, API gateways

**Storing and scaling data**
- Partitioning (sharding): how you split data, and what breaks when you do
- Replication: leader–follower, and the lag that comes with it
- Choosing storage: relational, key-value, document, blob, search index
- Consistency models: strong, eventual, and what each costs

**Making it fast and reliable**
- Caching: where, what to evict, and how to invalidate
- Asynchronous work: queues, event streams, and back-pressure
- Resilience: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, graceful degradation
- Probabilistic structures — Bloom filters and friends, and when they are the right answer

**Doing it in an interview**
- Driving a design end to end in 45 minutes, in a repeatable order
- Defending trade-offs when the interviewer pushes back — which is the actual assessment

### Why this is enough

A system design interview is always the same shape: **clarify requirements → estimate scale → sketch
the components → go deep on one or two → defend the trade-offs.** The topics above are what you need
to have opinions about at each of those steps.

There is no depth ceiling in this subject — real distributed systems are a career. The interview
version is bounded, and the bound is roughly: can you reason about scale out loud, choose sensibly,
and explain what you gave up.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Gaurav Sen — System Design for Beginners | **LEARN** | 5 | Free five-hour orientation. The vocabulary |
| 2 | Hello Interview — System Design in a Hurry | **LEARN** | 15 | Free, and the closest thing to an answer key |
| 3 | System Design Interview Vol 1 (Alex Xu) | **LEARN** | 10 | One chapter per classic problem |
| 4 | Designing Data-Intensive Applications | **LEARN** | 6 | Four chapters only — the depth behind the answers |
| 5 | 6 timed designs vs expert breakdowns | **PRACTICE** | 14 | The only practice available |

---

## Say it plainly: these four do not form a ladder

Unlike databases, **there is no clean progression here.** These are four overlapping resources that
each do one thing well, and the honest framing is: use each for its job and accept the overlap.

- **Gaurav Sen** is orientation. Watch it once, early, to learn what the words mean. It is not a
  syllabus and rewatching it will not help.
- **Hello Interview** is the framework — how to *run* the 45 minutes — plus worked breakdowns of
  common problems. This is the one to lean on.
- **Alex Xu** is a problem bank: one chapter per classic design. Use it as an answer key, one problem
  at a time, not as a book to read.
- **DDIA** is where the real depth is, and it is a 600-page book. Take **four chapters only** —
  replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency. Reading it all is genuinely worthwhile and is
  not what this year is for.

**If you only have time for two: Hello Interview and the timed practice.** Everything else is
enrichment.

---

# The order

## Month 1 (of this subject — around month 6 overall): orientation, once

> **LEARN — Gaurav Sen**, five hours, watched once, early.

You are learning vocabulary: what a load balancer is, what sharding means, why caching is not free.
Do not take notes as if it were a course.

## Then, the core loop — and it is a loop, not a sequence

> **LEARN — Hello Interview** interleaved with **PRACTICE — timed designs**

Read one section of Hello Interview's framework, then **immediately design something with it**, cold,
45 minutes, nothing open. Only after your attempt, read their breakdown of the same problem and note
**every question you failed to ask.**

That last part is the whole exercise. In system design, the questions you did not ask are the
assessment — not the diagram you drew.

Six timed designs, roughly one a week.

> **LEARN — Alex Xu** supplies the problems when you want one Hello Interview has not covered. One
> chapter per attempt, read strictly after.

## In parallel, slowly: the depth reading

> **LEARN — DDIA, four chapters**

Replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency. Read these across the whole period, not as a
block. They are what let you answer the follow-up question rather than the first one.

## Ongoing

One design a month keeps it alive. This subject decays fast because it is entirely reasoning and no
muscle memory.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | ~1.5 | Gaurav Sen once · Hello Interview begins | First cold design |
| **7–8** | **~3.9** | Hello Interview · Alex Xu chapters · DDIA's four | **Six timed designs vs the breakdowns** |
| 9–10 | ~0.9 | — | One design a month |

---

## What a session looks like

**A design session (110 minutes):** 45 minutes designing cold on a blank page — requirements,
estimates, components, one deep dive. Then read the expert breakdown and spend 30 minutes listing
what you missed. Then 20 minutes redoing the weakest part.

**A reading session (60 minutes):** one Hello Interview section or one DDIA chapter, with a specific
design problem in mind that it applies to.

---

## Honest warnings

**Nothing here can grade you**, so the temptation to read four books and call it done is stronger than
in any other subject. The expert breakdowns are the closest available substitute for a judge — use
them *after* attempting, always.

**Do not start DDIA as a book you intend to finish.** It is superb and it is 600 pages. Four chapters
is the plan; the rest is for a year when you have time.

**Practising this without a clock is close to useless.** Given unlimited time, everyone produces a
reasonable architecture. The interview is 45 minutes.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. Six designs completed cold in 45 minutes each, then compared against an expert version
2. You reach for estimation numbers automatically, out loud, before designing
3. When pushed on a choice, you name what you gave up rather than defending the choice
4. You can explain replication lag, and one specific bug it causes, without notes
5. The gap between your attempt and the expert breakdown is shrinking — that is the real measure

# Python & Its Data Libraries

**~53 hours.** Not a first language — a second one, learned properly, because both projects in this
plan are built in it and because "knows Python" on a CV is a promise someone will test.

---

## Why this is in the plan

Two reasons.

**It is the prerequisite for the projects.** The backend service and the retrieval service are both
Python, and building them while still fighting the language wastes the project hours.

**Claiming it invites questions.** If Python is on your CV, an interviewer may ask what a decorator
is, how a generator differs from a list, or why a mutable default argument is a trap. Those are not
obscure — they are the standard checks for whether "Python" means "wrote a script once".

---

## What's covered

**The language properly**
- Data model and the special methods that make your objects behave like built-in ones
- Iterators, generators, and why laziness matters
- Decorators and closures · Context managers · Comprehensions
- Mutable default arguments, late binding, and the other standard traps

**The professional layer**
- Type hints and a type checker · Virtual environments and dependency management
- Testing with pytest · Formatting and linting

**Concurrency, and its peculiarities here**
- Threads, processes, and async — and why Python's choice between them is unusual

**The data libraries**
- NumPy — arrays, broadcasting, why loops are slow and vectors are not
- pandas — selection, grouping, joining, reshaping
- Enough SciPy to not be surprised by it

**For the projects specifically**
- Pydantic for validation · SQLAlchemy for talking to a database

### Why this list is enough

Python interview questions come in two flavours: *do you know the language beyond scripting* — the
first group — and *can you use it professionally* — the second. The data libraries are separate and
only matter if they are on your CV, in which case they matter a lot, because "used pandas" is very
easy to check.

Deliberately excluded: web frameworks, which are covered inside the backend project where they
belong, and machine-learning libraries, which are a different subject entirely.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Exercism Python track | **PRACTICE** | 10 | Graded exercises, plus free human mentoring |
| 2 | Fluent Python (parts I, III, V) | **LEARN** | 18 | The book that takes you past scripting |
| 3 | pandas & NumPy official user guides | **LEARN** | 8 | Better than any course, and free |
| 4 | Written Python reference | **REFERENCE** | 0 | Syntax you have forgotten |

---

# The order

## Start with practice, not with the book

> **PRACTICE — Exercism's Python track**, from week one

Solve, submit, and read the community solutions afterwards. The exercises are graded automatically,
and **free human mentoring is available and is the most underused thing on the site.**

Starting here rather than with the book is deliberate: it finds out what you actually do not know,
rather than assuming.

## Alongside it: the book, but only three parts

> **LEARN — Fluent Python**, parts I, III and V only

The data model, functions as first-class objects, and control flow — that is where the difference
between scripting and knowing the language lives. **Type out every example.** Skip the rest of the
book for now; it is excellent and it is not this year's problem.

## Then, once the language is comfortable: the data libraries

> **LEARN — the official pandas and NumPy user guides**

Read with a notebook open and **run every snippet on your own data rather than theirs.** The official
guides are genuinely better than the paid courses and cost nothing.

**Do not start these until Fluent Python's part I is done.** pandas is a large API surface, and
learning it on top of shaky language fundamentals produces someone who can copy recipes and not debug
them.

## The reference: never scheduled

> **REFERENCE — the written Python reference.** Look-up only.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | LEARN | PRACTICE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | ~1 | Fluent Python part I | Exercism, steadily |
| **3–4** | **~3.6–4** | Fluent Python III & V · then pandas/NumPy guides | Exercism continues · library work on real data |
| 5–10 | ~0.3–0.6 | — | Python is now used *inside* the projects |

**After month 4 this subject mostly stops being studied and starts being used.** That is the intended
end state.

---

## What a session looks like

**A 60-minute session:** one Exercism exercise solved and submitted, then read two community
solutions to the same problem. The second half is where most of the learning is — Python has strong
idioms, and reading them is how you acquire them.

**A library session (75 minutes):** one section of the pandas guide, applied immediately to a dataset
you actually care about.

---

## Honest warnings

**Do not learn pandas from video courses.** The official user guide is better, free, and current.

**If pandas or NumPy are on your CV, this subject is not optional.** "Used pandas" is one of the
easiest claims to check — one question about a chained-assignment warning or a groupby-apply and it
becomes obvious.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. Write a decorator and a context manager from scratch, no reference
2. Explain generators versus lists, with a case where the difference actually matters
3. Name three standard Python traps and why each happens
4. Do a groupby-aggregate-join in pandas without looking anything up
5. Both projects being written without the language slowing you down
