# Building a Real Backend Service

**~98 hours — the single biggest project in this plan, and the highest-leverage thing in it.**

One service, built properly rather than quickly, that makes about twenty separate CV claims true at
once.

---

## Why this exists

Most CVs list a stack: a language, a framework, a database, containers, a cloud provider, testing,
continuous integration. Most of those lines, examined, turn out to mean "followed a tutorial once".

The efficient fix is not twenty small exercises. **It is one service, built the way a working
engineer would build it**, because doing that touches all twenty naturally and gives you something
deployed you can point at.

It is also the answer to the most common interview opening: *"tell me about something you built."*

---

## What it covers

Roughly twenty skills, and this is deliberately the same list as a typical backend job advert:

**The service itself** — web framework · database access and an ORM · schema migrations ·
authentication and authorisation · request validation · background jobs · caching · file/object
storage · API documentation · rate limiting

**Making it professional** — automated tests · linting and formatting · continuous integration ·
containerisation · configuration and secrets · structured logging and metrics

**Getting it live** — a reverse proxy · deployment to a real host · a health check · a public URL that
stays up

### Why one project rather than twenty exercises

Because the connections *are* the skill. Anyone can add authentication to a tutorial. Adding it to a
service that already has migrations, tests and a deployment — and keeping all of those working — is
the actual job, and it is what the follow-up questions probe.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The project itself | **PRACTICE** | 98 | Build it. There is no reading here |

The framework documentation you will need — the web framework, the database library, the container
tool, the host — is looked up as you go. **There is no course for this and you should not go looking
for one.**

---

# The order

The order below is not arbitrary. Each step is chosen so the next one is possible, and so that the
thing is deployed and working from very early on.

## Step 0 — decide the scope, and build nothing

**One page, before any code:** what the service does, and the list of CV claims it must make true.

Spend a session on this. Getting the scope wrong costs a hundred hours, and the standard failure is
choosing something too ambitious and abandoning it at 60%. **A small service, finished and deployed,
beats an ambitious one that is not.**

## Step 1 — make it real before you make it good

1. **A minimal working service with one endpoint**
2. **A real database behind it**, with migrations from the very first table — retrofitting migrations
   later is genuinely painful
3. **Containerise it** — early, so it never "works only on my machine"
4. **Deploy it, publicly, with a health check** — a real URL, in week one or two

**Deploying this early is the most important sequencing decision here.** A project that is deployed
from the start stays deployable. A project deployed at the end usually is not, and that is where
these efforts die.

## Step 2 — make it correct

5. **Tests**, then **continuous integration** so they run on every push
6. **Request validation** — reject bad input properly, at the edge
7. **Authentication and authorisation** — and know the difference, because you will be asked

## Step 3 — make it professional

8. **Structured logging** with a request identifier that follows a request through
9. **A metrics endpoint** · **rate limiting** · **caching**, where it is actually needed
10. **Background jobs** for work that should not block a response
11. **Configuration and secrets** handled properly — nothing hard-coded, nothing committed
12. **API documentation**, generated rather than written by hand

## Step 4 — prove it

13. **Write the README as if a stranger will run it**, because the point is that someone will
14. **Go through the OWASP Top 10** against your own service
15. **Break it on purpose**: kill the database and see what the service does. Send it ten times the
    traffic. Whatever happens is your answer to "how does it fail?"

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | What is happening |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | ~0.5 | Scope on one page. Nothing built |
| 3 | ~2.8 | Steps 1–2: service, database, container, **deployed** |
| 4 | ~3.8 | Step 2 finished: tests, CI, auth |
| 5 | ~6 | Step 3: the professional layer |
| **6** | **~8.2** | **Ships. Live URL, tests green, README done** |
| 7–10 | ~0.5 | Keep it alive. Fix what breaks |

**It ships at the end of month 6, and that date is load-bearing** — it is the last high-capacity
month, and every later month assumes this is done.

---

## What a session looks like

**A 90-minute session:** one item from the list above, finished and deployed before you stop. Not
half-finished and left. **The project should be in a working, deployed state at the end of every
session** — that constraint is what stops it becoming an abandoned branch.

---

## Honest warnings

**The biggest risk is scope, not difficulty.** Pick something small enough to finish. A well-built
service that does one thing will out-argue an ambitious half-built one in every interview.

**Deploy in week one.** Everything about this gets harder if deployment is left until the end.

**Do not restart it.** Around month 4 you will know enough to see that your early choices were poor,
and the urge to start again will be strong. Refactor instead. Restarting is how this project dies.

**Do not follow a tutorial for the whole thing.** Look things up per step. A tutorial produces a
service you cannot defend, which is worse than no project at all.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. A stranger can clone it, follow the README, and run it
2. It is deployed at a public URL, with a health check, and it has been up for a month
3. Continuous integration runs the tests on every push and has caught a real mistake
4. You can explain every dependency you added and why
5. You can answer "what happens when the database goes away?" — because you tried it
6. Every one of the twenty CV lines it covers is a line you can defend in detail

# AI Engineering — Retrieval & Evaluation

**~64 hours.** Build a system that answers questions from your own documents — and, more importantly,
build the thing that measures whether it answers them *well*.

---

## Why this is in the plan

Because it is currently the cheapest genuine differentiator available.

Almost every company is doing something in this area, most people applying have either nothing or a
weekend chatbot demo, and the bar for "has actually built one" is low enough to clear in sixty hours.

**The differentiator is not the retrieval. It is the evaluation.** Anyone can wire a language model to
a document store. Being able to say "here is how I measured it, here is what it scored, here is what
I changed and by how much it improved" is a different conversation, and it is the one that sounds
like engineering rather than like a demo.

---

## What it covers

**Retrieval**
- Embeddings and vector search — what a vector store is actually doing
- Chunking documents, and why chunk size quietly decides your quality ceiling
- Hybrid search — combining keyword and semantic matching, which beats either alone
- Re-ranking the results before they go to the model

**Using the model properly**
- Structured output and tool use · Prompt and context construction
- Guardrails — refusing to answer rather than inventing

**The part that matters**
- Building an evaluation set and scoring against it
- Choosing metrics that mean something for your task
- Tracing a request end to end, so a bad answer can be diagnosed
- Cost and latency — the constraints that make it a real system

### Why this is enough

A retrieval system is: **get the right documents, give them to a model well, and know whether the
answer was good.** Those are the three groups. Everything fashionable in this area is a variation on
one of them.

Deliberately excluded: training or fine-tuning models. That is a different job, needs different
hardware, and is not what most companies are hiring for.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The project itself | **PRACTICE** | 64 | Build it |
| 2 | Hamel Husain's writing on evaluation | **LEARN** | included | The best free material on evaluating these systems |

---

# The order

**Build retrieval first and evaluation second — but treat evaluation as the real deliverable.**

## Step 1 — the simplest thing that works
Documents in, chunked, embedded, stored. A question comes in, the closest chunks come out, the model
answers using them. **Keep it deliberately basic.** You need a baseline before you can improve
anything.

## Step 2 — the evaluation harness, before any improvements
Write thirty to fifty questions with known good answers. Score your baseline against them. **This is
the step everyone skips and it is the entire value of the project.**

Without it, every later change is a guess. With it, you can say "chunk size 500 scored 0.62, chunk
size 200 with overlap scored 0.71" — and that sentence is the interview.

## Step 3 — improve, measured
Now change things, one at a time, re-scoring after each: chunk size and overlap, hybrid search,
re-ranking, prompt structure. **Keep the numbers.** The record of what you tried and what it did is
worth more than the final score.

## Step 4 — make it a system
Tracing, so a bad answer can be diagnosed. Guardrails, so it declines rather than invents. Cost and
latency measured per request.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | What is happening |
|---|---|---|
| 7–8 | ~4.6 | Steps 1–3: baseline, evaluation harness, measured improvements |
| 9–10 | ~3 | Step 4, and writing up what you tried |

---

## Honest warnings

**Do not build a chatbot.** Everyone has one. Build the measurement.

**Do not adopt a large framework first.** They hide exactly the parts you are trying to demonstrate
you understand. Write the retrieval loop yourself; it is not much code.

**Keep the experiment log.** The changes you tried and their measured effect are the artefact. Losing
that and keeping only the final version throws away the good half.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. An evaluation set exists, and you can quote your score on it
2. You can name three changes you made and what each did to the score
3. A bad answer can be traced back to which retrieved chunk caused it
4. You know what one query costs and how long it takes
5. It refuses to answer when it should, and you can show that happening

# Systems Programming

**~44 hours.** Build small versions of tools you use every day: a word counter, a text searcher, a
shell, and an HTTP server.

---

## Why this is in the plan

Because "build your own X" is asked far more often than its reputation suggests — around a quarter of
the interview accounts collected involved building a scaled-down version of some real tool. And
because these four projects teach, by force, the things that operating systems and networks teach in
theory.

You cannot write a shell without understanding process creation. You cannot write an HTTP server
without understanding sockets. The concepts stop being definitions.

---

## What it covers

- **Reading files and streams efficiently** — buffering, and why it matters
- **Scanning text and matching patterns** — how a regular-expression engine actually works
- **Process control** — creating processes, connecting them with pipes, waiting for them
- **Sockets and servers** — accepting connections, handling more than one at a time
- **Wire protocols** — parsing a request, forming a response, handling malformed input

### Why four projects is enough

They are chosen so each needs the one before it. File reading → text scanning → process control →
networking. By the fourth you have touched every layer between a file on disk and a response on a
socket, which is the whole surface these questions come from.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Four build-your-own projects | **PRACTICE** | 44 | In order: wc → grep → shell → HTTP server |
| 2 | Coding Challenges (the problem list) | **REFERENCE** | 0 | Specifications for each |

---

# The order — strictly sequential

**1. A word counter.** Count lines, words, bytes. Then make it fast on a very large file, and find out
what buffering does. *Teaches: file input, buffering, command-line arguments.*

**2. A text searcher.** Match a fixed string, then simple patterns. *Teaches: string algorithms and
how pattern matching is actually implemented.*

**3. A shell.** Read a command, run it, wait for it. Then add pipes between commands, then background
jobs. *Teaches: process creation, file descriptors, signals — the operating-systems subject, made
concrete.*

**4. An HTTP server.** Accept a connection, parse the request, serve a file. Then handle several
clients at once. *Teaches: sockets, protocol parsing, concurrency.*

**Do them in this order and do not skip.** Each supplies something the next needs, and the fourth is
much harder without the third.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | What is happening |
|---|---|---|
| 1–4 | ~0.8–1.2 | Word counter, then text searcher. Evenings work |
| 5–8 | ~0.4 | Slow progress on the shell — other things dominate |
| **9–10** | **~2.6** | Shell finished, HTTP server built |

---

## Honest warnings

**These are addictive and can eat the plan.** Each has an obvious "next feature". Stop when the
project does the core job; the learning is in the first version, not the polish.

**Do not look at the real implementations first.** They are decades of optimisation and will make
your version look pointless. Build yours, then read theirs.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. All four run and do their core job
2. Your shell handles a pipeline of two commands correctly
3. Your server serves two simultaneous clients without breaking
4. You can explain what happens, end to end, when someone types a piped command into your shell

# Defending Everything on Your CV

**~58 hours, concentrated in the final two months.** Every line on your CV is a question you have
agreed to answer. This is where you find out which ones you cannot.

---

## Why this gets 58 hours

Because the most avoidable way to lose an interview is to be caught out on something you wrote about
yourself.

A typical CV lists fifteen to twenty technologies. Audited honestly, the usual split is roughly a
third you can genuinely discuss in depth, a third you can discuss for one question and not two, and a
third you used once and cannot defend at all. **That last third is not neutral — it is a liability**,
because the interviewer has no way to know which third they are asking about, and being caught on one
line casts doubt on all the others.

---

## What's covered

- **The audit** — three hard questions per line, answered in writing
- **The numbers** — re-deriving every figure you quote
- **The gaps** — closing what the audit exposes, hardest first
- **The rehearsal** — hostile questioning until nothing surprises you
- **The ranking** — deciding what stays, what is reworded, and what is removed

### Why this is enough

There is no external syllabus here. Your CV *is* the syllabus, and it is finite. The work is entirely
mechanical: enumerate, interrogate, close or remove.

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | CV audit — three questions per line | **PRACTICE** | 20 | Find out what you cannot defend |
| 2 | Re-derive every number you quote | **PRACTICE** | 6 | Make sure the figures are real |
| 3 | Close the gaps the audit exposes | **PRACTICE** | 15 | The point of doing the audit |
| 4 | Adversarial mock interview against an LLM | **PRACTICE** | 4 | Cheap, repeatable hostile questioning |

All practice. There is nothing to learn — only things to find out.

---

# The order

## Step 1 — the honest column
Write every technology and claim from your CV in a single column. Next to each, answer honestly:
could you answer three questions about this right now? Mark each solid, partial, or absent.

**Do this before anything else, and do it early — not in the last two months.** The output determines
what the rest of the plan should have been prioritising, which is only useful if there is time left.

## Step 2 — the audit
For each line, write the three hardest questions someone could ask, and answer them **in writing**.
Writing matters: it is the difference between believing you could answer and finding out.

## Step 3 — re-derive the numbers
Any percentage, speedup or scale figure you quote — work it out again from scratch. If you cannot
reproduce it, change the claim. This is the fastest way to lose credibility and the easiest to
prevent.

## Step 4 — close the gaps, hardest first
Work through what the audit found. Some gaps close in an hour; some need a small project. Some should
be closed by **removing the line**, and that is a legitimate and underused option.

## Step 5 — rehearse adversarially
Paste your CV into a language model and ask to be interrogated as hostilely as possible. Cheap,
repeatable, and it finds soft lines fast. Then do it with a person.

---

## The whole thing in one table

| Months | h/week | What is happening |
|---|---|---|
| 1–6 | ~0.5 | The honest column, early. Then slow chipping at the worst lines |
| 7 | ~0.8 | Audit begins in earnest |
| **9–10** | **~4.2** | **The full audit, gap-closing, and rehearsal** |

---

## Honest warnings

**Do the honest column in month one, not month nine.** Its whole value is telling you what to
prioritise, and by month nine there is no time left to act on it.

**Removing a line is a real answer.** A shorter CV you can defend completely is stronger than a long
one with three landmines in it.

---

## TEST — how to know you're done

1. Every line has three written questions with written answers
2. Every number you quote has been re-derived
3. No line remains that you would rather not be asked about
4. A hostile mock interview produces no surprises
briefs.D06:
# Talking About Your Own Projects

**~24 hours.** Distinct from defending your CV's technology list: this is about the projects
themselves, and it is asked in roughly 95% of interviews.

---

## Why this matters more than its hours suggest

"Tell me about a project" is the most reliably asked question in any interview, and the one people
prepare for least, because they assume knowing the project is the same as being able to talk about
it. It is not.

The failure is specific: interviewers find the seam by **asking one level down.** Why that database?
What did you try first? What would you do differently? What broke? Answers stop being fluent very
quickly, and the interviewer learns something about how much of the work was actually yours.

---

## What's covered

- **The ownership map** — which parts you wrote, which you integrated, which you copied
- **The decision log** — three real decisions per project, and the alternatives you rejected
- **The failure story** — one thing that went wrong, what you did, what you learned
- **Deep-dive readiness** — being able to go two levels down on any component
- **Your own background story** — why this field, coherently, if you are switching
- **Adversarial rehearsal**

---

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Write an ownership map, decision log and failure story | **PRACTICE** | 24 | Written down, not remembered |

---

# The order

**Write, do not rehearse.** For each project: the ownership map first (it is uncomfortable and
clarifying), then three decisions with rejected alternatives, then one failure with what you did.

Then have someone — or a language model — ask *why* three times in a row on each answer. Where you
run out of road is exactly where an interviewer will find you.

Half an hour a week, all year. This decays fast because the project keeps receding.

---

## TEST

1. An ownership map exists for each project, in writing, and it is honest
2. Three decisions per project, each with the alternative you rejected and why
3. One failure story that ends in something you changed
4. You survive "why?" three times in a row on any component

# Java

**~27 hours.** A second language, learned from a C++ starting point, because a meaningful share of
companies test in it and some interviews are Java-only.

---

## Why it is here at all

Not because Java is better, but because it removes a filter. Some companies will only interview in
Java, some assessments give Java-only templates, and enterprise backend roles are disproportionately
Java. Twenty-seven hours removes that constraint entirely.

## What's covered

- Syntax and collections, coming from C++ — mostly a translation exercise
- **How memory works differently** — garbage collection, and what it means for how you write code
- **The equals and hashCode contract** — a genuine interview favourite, and easy to get wrong
- Building one REST service with Spring Boot

### Why this is enough

You are not becoming a Java specialist. You need to write clean idiomatic Java in an interview and
answer questions about the two things Java-focused interviewers always ask: memory management and
object equality.

## The resources at a glance

| # | Resource | Label | Hours | One-line job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Oracle's official Java tutorial | **LEARN** | 10 | Syntax and collections from a C++ base |
| 2 | Spring Boot official guides | **LEARN** | 15 | One working REST service |

# The order

**Skim what transfers, slow down on what does not.** Loops and classes are familiar; garbage
collection, the collections framework's design, and equality semantics are not — spend the time
there.

Then **follow one Spring Boot guide end to end** until a service runs. Breadth across many guides is
worth far less than one that actually works.

## TEST

1. Solve two algorithm problems in Java, comfortably, without fighting the syntax
2. Explain the equals and hashCode contract and what breaks when it is violated
3. Explain in outline how garbage collection affects how you write code
4. One Spring Boot REST service running locally

# Aptitude & Puzzles

**~6 hours.** Small, and occasionally eliminatory — some companies gate the technical round behind an
aptitude test, so failing it means your coding never gets seen.

## What's covered
Arithmetic, ratios and interest · time, work and speed · permutations, combinations and probability ·
progressions and algebra · geometry · clocks and calendars · series and analogy · coding-decoding ·
blood relations and directions · syllogisms and Venn diagrams · seating puzzles · data interpretation ·
mental arithmetic · expected value and simple game theory · estimation.

**Why this is enough:** aptitude tests are drawn from a fixed and well-known pool. The list above is
that pool. The skill being tested is speed, not depth.

## The resources at a glance
| # | Resource | Label | Hours | Job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Written aptitude reference (37 topics) | **LEARN** | 5 | Revision plus timed sets |
| 2 | GeeksforGeeks top-100 puzzles | **PRACTICE** | 1 | The puzzles that actually get asked |

# The order
**Always against a clock.** Untimed aptitude practice trains the wrong thing entirely. Half an hour
a week, one topic at a time, timed. For puzzles, say your reasoning out loud — that is what is being
assessed in the room.

## TEST
1. A full mock aptitude test cleared within its time limit
2. Mental arithmetic fast enough that it is not the bottleneck
briefs.D10:
# Behavioural Interviews

**~4 hours.** Asked in roughly 80% of interviews and prepared for by almost nobody, which makes it
unusually cheap to be good at.

## What's covered
The STAR structure — Situation, Task, Action, Result · conflict · failure and recovery · leading
without authority · why this company · why software · strengths and weaknesses · questions to ask
them · offer conversations.

**Why four stories is enough:** every behavioural question is a variation on conflict, failure,
leadership, or ambiguity. Four well-chosen real situations, each covering one theme, answer almost
anything — you re-frame rather than invent.

## The resources at a glance
| # | Resource | Label | Hours | Job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Write 4 STAR stories, mapped to common themes | **PRACTICE** | 4 | Written, not improvised |

# The order
Write four real situations out in full — Situation, Task, Action, Result — then check each covers a
different theme. **Write them down.** Improvising a structured answer under pressure is much harder
than it sounds, and the result is usually a rambling account with no result at the end.

## TEST
1. Four written stories, each ending in a concrete result
2. Each covers a distinct theme
3. Any behavioural question maps to one of them within a few seconds

# Everyday Tools — Git, Regex, Debuggers

**~5 hours.** Rarely a topic on its own; constantly assumed. Being slow with these is visible in a
pair-programming round and expensive every day of a job.

## What's covered
Git's object model · branching and merging · rewriting history safely · finding a bad commit by
bisection · collaboration workflows · regular expressions · shell basics and scripting · using a
debugger properly · build systems.

**Why this is enough:** these are the tools you touch hourly. The bar is fluency, not expertise, and
five hours of deliberate practice gets there because most of the gap is habit rather than knowledge.

## The resources at a glance
| # | Resource | Label | Hours | Job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Learn Git Branching | **PRACTICE** | 2 | Interactive, visual, in the browser |
| 2 | Pro Git, chapters 7 and 10 | **LEARN** | 2 | The tools you have not used, and what git does underneath |
| 3 | Write and test 10 regular expressions | **PRACTICE** | 1 | Against real text, including cases that should fail |

# The order
Do the interactive tutorial first — it teaches branching and rebasing visually in about two hours,
far faster than reading. Then Pro Git chapter 7 for the tools you have never used, and chapter 10 for
what git is actually doing, which is what you need when something goes wrong.

## TEST
1. Rebase, cherry-pick and bisect without looking anything up
2. Recover a commit you deleted
3. Write a working regular expression for a real problem, first try
briefs.D12:
# Computer Networks

**~6 hours.** Asked in about a quarter of interviews, usually as a small number of standard questions.

## What's covered
The layered model · TCP versus UDP · the three-way handshake · flow and congestion control · sockets ·
HTTP and its versions · DNS · TLS · addressing and network address translation · the diagnostic tools ·
load balancing.

**Why this is enough:** network questions in software interviews cluster tightly — what happens when
you type a URL, TCP versus UDP, how HTTPS works. The list above covers that cluster with room to
spare, and anything deeper belongs to a networking role.

## The resources at a glance
| # | Resource | Label | Hours | Job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Beej's Guide to Network Programming | **LEARN** | 4 | The standard free introduction |
| 2 | Inspect real traffic — Wireshark, dig, curl | **PRACTICE** | 2 | See an actual connection happen |

# The order
Read Beej's guide **while writing the socket code it describes**. Then watch a real connection: resolve
a name with `dig`, make a request with `curl -v`, and look at an actual handshake in Wireshark.

**Seeing one real handshake is worth more than any amount of reading about it**, which is why two of
the six hours are practice.

## TEST
1. Explain what happens when you type a URL, end to end, including DNS and TLS
2. Say when you would choose UDP, with a real example
3. Read a packet capture of a connection being established
briefs.D13:
# Knowing What AI Terms Mean

**~3 hours.** The smallest subject here, and deliberately so.

## Why it is so small
The measured demand is far lower than the noise suggests — around 6% of interviews, and mostly as
conversation rather than assessment. Its purpose is **conversational fluency, not capability**: being
able to discuss what a language model is doing, what retrieval-augmented generation means, and what
evaluation involves, without either overclaiming or looking lost.

Actual capability in this area comes from the retrieval project, not from here.

## What's covered
Classical machine learning in outline · what the common metrics mean · neural networks in outline ·
transformers and language models · retrieval-augmented generation · evaluation · prompt and context
construction · how these systems are deployed and monitored.

## The resources at a glance
| # | Resource | Label | Hours | Job |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Chip Huyen — how a generative-AI platform fits together | **LEARN** | 3 | Vocabulary, once |

# The order
One read, near the end of the plan. If your CV claims machine-learning work, this is not enough and
those claims belong in the CV-defence subject instead.

## TEST
1. Explain retrieval-augmented generation to a non-technical person
2. Say what you would measure to know whether such a system is working
3. Not overclaim — the correct answer to a deep question is often "I have not built that"
briefs.D15:
# University Coursework

**~37 hours across four subjects** — computer architecture, digital electronics and VLSI, hardware
description languages, and GPU architecture.

## What this is, and what it is not
**Exam-pass level, no further.** These are degree requirements, not interview preparation. They
appear in this plan only so they do not silently consume time that belongs elsewhere.

The exception worth knowing: **computer architecture genuinely helps** — caches, memory hierarchy and
alignment explain why some code is fast and some is slow, and that does come up. The rest is degree
work.

## The order
Whatever your exam schedule demands, at the level a good grade requires. Do not extend it. If a topic
here also appears in a software interview, it is covered better in another subject in this guide.

## TEST
Passing your exams with the grade you want. That is the entire criterion.

# Working Like a Professional Engineer

**Covered inside the backend project — no separate hours.**

## What it means
Reading unfamiliar code · reviewing someone else's · writing down why a decision was made · managing
dependencies · shipping behind a flag · **getting one change merged into a project you do not own**.

## The one thing to do separately
**Get a single pull request merged into someone else's open-source project.** Small is fine — a
documentation fix counts. What you learn is the part that never appears in your own projects: reading
a codebase you did not write, following its conventions, and responding to review.

## TEST
One merged pull request in a repository you do not own.
briefs.D26:
# Application Security

**Covered inside the backend project — no separate hours.**

## What it means
The OWASP Top 10 · authentication versus authorisation · token handling mistakes · password storage ·
injection, cross-site scripting and request forgery · secrets management · TLS basics · dependency
risk.

## The order
Read the OWASP Top 10 once — it is a short list and free — then go through your own service and check
it against each item. **Finding a real vulnerability in your own code is worth more than any amount of
reading**, and it is a good interview story.

## TEST
1. Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation without hesitating
2. Name three specific vulnerabilities and how you prevented each in your own service
briefs.D27:
# Running Software in Production

**Covered inside the backend project — no separate hours.**

## What it means
Structured logging with an identifier that follows a request · a metrics endpoint · tracing · health
checks · alerting · what to do during an incident · service level objectives.

## The order
Build it into the service as you go, not afterwards. Then **break your own service on purpose** and
find out whether your logs and metrics would have told you what happened. If they would not, they are
decoration.

## TEST
1. A request can be traced end to end through your logs by its identifier

briefs.D28:
# Deployment & Cloud

**Covered inside the backend project — no separate hours.**

## What it means
Deploying to one platform properly · environment configuration · persistent storage and backups ·
zero-downtime deploys · object storage · infrastructure as code, in outline.

## The order
**One platform, end to end, early.** Depth on one beats a superficial tour of three. Deploy in the
first week of the project and keep it deployed — everything about this is harder if it is left to the
end.

Kubernetes is deliberately excluded. It is a large subject, rarely needed at this stage, and easy to
learn later once the fundamentals are real.

## TEST
1. A public URL that has stayed up for a month
2. You can deploy a change with no downtime
3. You know what happens to your data if the machine disappears
briefs.D23:
# Concurrency & Distributed Systems

**Covered inside the backend project — no separate hours.**

## What it means
Thread safety in real code · asynchronous versus threaded models · the failure modes of distributed
work · idempotency and delivery guarantees · replication and consensus in outline · profiling.

## Where it actually gets learned
The theory is in *Operating Systems & Concurrency* and *Designing a Whole System*. What the backend
project adds is the part theory cannot teach: **making a real endpoint safe to call twice**, retrying
without duplicating, and finding out what your service does when something downstream is slow.

## TEST
1. An endpoint in your service that is safe to call twice, and you can explain why
2. A retry that does not duplicate work
3. You have profiled your own service and found a real bottleneck
briefs.D16:
# University Coursework

**~37 hours across four subjects** — computer architecture, digital electronics and VLSI, hardware
description languages, and GPU architecture.

## What this is, and what it is not
**Exam-pass level, no further.** These are degree requirements, not interview preparation. They
appear in this plan only so they do not silently consume time that belongs elsewhere.

The exception worth knowing: **computer architecture genuinely helps** — caches, memory hierarchy and
alignment explain why some code is fast and some is slow, and that does come up. The rest is degree
work.

## The order
Whatever your exam schedule demands, at the level a good grade requires. Do not extend it. If a topic
here also appears in a software interview, it is covered better in another subject in this guide.

## TEST
Passing your exams with the grade you want. That is the entire criterion.
